query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing interstitial oxygen and nitrogen to ultra-low levels via non-alloying getter-assisted ultra-high-vacuum annealing, followed by controlled recrystallization to clean equiaxed grains, will convert the predominantly intergranular, brittle room-temperature response of equiatomic NbMoTaW into measurable ductility without degrading its single-phase BCC stability, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance, or ion-irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Nb25Mo25Ta25W25, single-phase BCC, as-cast polycrystalline with typical interstitial content (O+N) in the 10^2–10^3 wt ppm range and mixed grain sizes; poor RT ductility; high compressive strength at 1600 °C; irradiation resistance primarily predicted by first-principles.
generation.intervention: Non-alloying interstitial scavenging by high-temperature ultra-high-vacuum annealing with external Ti/Zr getter foils (physically separated from the sample to avoid diffusion), followed by a short recrystallization anneal to form clean 10–50 µm equiaxed grains.
generation.conditions: Primary getter anneal: 1700–1800 °C, 4–8 h, ≤1e-7 Torr UHV, sample enclosed with Ti/Zr getter foils but not in contact; immediate cool under vacuum. Secondary recrystallization: 1100–1250 °C, 0.5–2 h, high vacuum or inert Ar, then air-cool. Final surface polish to remove any adsorbates.
generation.structural_mediator: Substantially reduced bulk and grain-boundary oxygen/nitrogen content (<~100 wt ppm total), diminished interstitial segregation at grain boundaries, cleaner boundaries with improved cohesion, and reduced dislocation pinning; retention of single-phase BCC solid solution.
generation.mechanism: In NbMoTaW, interstitial O/N segregate to boundaries and pin dislocations, promoting intergranular fracture and dynamic strain aging at RT. Getter annealing reduces interstitial content and boundary segregation, increasing grain-boundary cohesion and dislocation mobility, thereby enabling more homogeneous slip and measurable RT ductility. Because the refractory solid solution dominates high-temperature strength at 1600 °C, and no new phases are introduced, high-T performance remains within baseline. Cleaner boundaries and fewer interstitial-rich sites also limit irradiation-induced defect nucleation and segregation, preserving or slightly improving irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome:
- Room temperature: transition from near-zero elongation with intergranular fracture to measurable tensile ductility (uniform elongation increasing by a factor of a few), with a modest decrease in yield strength (likely <~20%) relative to baseline due to reduced interstitial pinning.
- 1600 °C: compressive strength and creep rate within ±10% of baseline; fracture mode and phase remain single-phase BCC.
- Irradiation (heavy-ion, e.g., Fe at 3 MeV to ~10 dpa, 300–500 °C): similar or slightly reduced irradiation-induced hardening and swelling compared to baseline; defect density and void nucleation not increased.
generation.baseline: As-cast equiatomic NbMoTaW without getter treatment, with typical interstitial levels and grain-boundary segregation, showing very poor RT ductility, excellent 1600 °C strength, and predicted irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: Effect requires achieving total O+N <~100 wt ppm and avoiding Ti/Zr diffusion into the alloy (>~0.3 at%) to maintain composition and single-phase BCC stability. Grain size should be in the 10–50 µm range; excessively fine grains (<~5 µm) may not improve RT ductility and excessively coarse grains (>~200 µm) may reduce uniform elongation. Exposure to oxidizing environments post-treatment can reintroduce embrittling interstitials and negate the effect. If the material contains secondary phases or carbide/nitride precipitates after processing, expected outcomes may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of RT ductility improvement depends on the starting interstitial content and achieved cleanliness; precise elongation changes cannot be predicted without measurement. The net effect on irradiation resistance is uncertain in the absence of direct experimental data (most reports are computational for this system). High-temperature creep may vary slightly with grain size; maintaining comparable grain size to baseline is important.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW specimens from the same melt: (i) baseline as-cast, (ii) getter-annealed and recrystallized as described. Verify that Ti/Zr did not alloy into the treated specimens (e.g., by EPMA/EDS). Quantify O/N by LECO gas analysis and grain-boundary chemistry by AES/TOF-SIMS. Conduct RT tensile tests (dog-bone geometry) and 1600 °C compression and creep tests under identical strain rates. Perform ion irradiation (e.g., 3 MeV Fe ions to ~10 dpa at 300–500 °C). Post-irradiation, measure nanoindentation hardness depth profiles and TEM of defect clusters/voids; assess swelling by cross-sectional TEM. Fractography (SEM) to classify fracture mode (intergranular vs transgranular).
measurements: RT tensile stress–strain (yield strength, uniform elongation, total elongation)
Post-irradiation nanoindentation hardness change vs depth
TEM defect density/void size and number density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (a) O+N is not reduced by at least ~50% versus baseline or grain-boundary O/N remains high, and RT tensile ductility does not increase by at least a factor of 2 at similar grain size; or (b) 1600 °C compressive strength decreases by >15% or creep rate increases by >20% compared to baseline; or (c) post-irradiation hardening or swelling increases by >20% relative to baseline.
